Well, uh... Just anybody could lead the row. If he could sing, it's all right. Doesn't matter who it was.
No... No name. I mean, you wouldn't call him a lead row?
No, sir.
Lead row man?
No, sir. Just like this, uh... So they got all different names. Some of them called shotguns. Some called pistol. Some called ratty red. Some called...
Mm-hmm.
Nose.
Yeah.
One gone. Guitar also. That's what they called me. Guitar.
Mm-hmm.
So... It's whatever come into your mind that they call you. That's it.
And what instruments did you play, speaking of guitar? You played some other ones?

No, sir. Well, when I first learned how to play, my grandfather had an old five-string banjo. Mm-hmm. And so... When those fellas leave our home, I'd take that old banjo and go in there and start to grab a phone. Oh, you know those grab phones used to wind up? You know, Charlie Jackson record on
and get behind him. Oh, yeah. Papa Charlie. That's right.

I'd get behind him. I'd hear him play, get the sound of his notes, go all by myself in the lot, in the barn, play. Sometime my mother would be looking for me and I wouldn't answer. Sometime it'd be 8 o'clock before I'd get out of that barn.
Shake that thing, huh?
Yes, sir. That's how I learned, just by myself. Nobody showed me.
What were some of the tunes you listened to?

Well, uh... Papa Lemon, this old piece by Blue Left Texas Lopey Like a Mule. I gave y'all that about the last time he always said. And then another one. Yeah. That's another one that he was playing. Sitting on top of the wall and all those old pieces.
Yeah, sir. Yeah. Testing, testing.

Let me know when you want to talk. I mean, when you're ready to cut it. I can ask you. Say, what was your grandfather's name? Bob Welch. Bob Welch. Yes, sir. Same as yours, just about. Yes, sir. Oh, I see. And, uh, did he play with bands?
No, sir. He was a preacher. He died a preacher.
And he played five-string banjo? Did he play it in church?
No, sir. He played, uh...
Did you get a chance to play?

Well, uh... He just had it around the house. Well, uh, he never... They'd go off playing on, but he just had it and had him a violin. So him and my mother, my grandmother, and we used to get together. He'd play the banjo and she'd play the violin. Then they'd change up. They'd have them old... Little old flang-dangs, as you call them.
Well, what kind of music would they play?
Well, uh, at that time, it was that old way back music.
Was it hymns, or was it simple songs?

Well, no, it was hymns. Yeah, okay. Calling what? Calling it. It figures. You know... Figures. Oh. Just go around the more round dances. You know, around the rang. Mm-hmm. They hold one other... Yeah.
Do you know, uh, any reels? What do you call reels? Quadrills, mazookas? No, sir. Those set dances is what you're talking about. Yes, sir. Do you know any of those?
No, sir, I don't. It's been so long.
You couldn't even give us a piece of one, huh?
I'll try to think of one.
Yeah, well, you know, if you could just give us a piece, it would be interesting to hear it.
I'll try to get through.

Come on. Good piece of one would be worth more than a whole bad song, you know? It's right, you know? Just a little bit of a good one would really be something. good. Uh... Now... Let me see now. You told about playing with some bands, and you say you played five-string banjo? Yes. Six-string guitar or twelve-string? Six-string guitar. Always. Yes, sir. And any other instruments?
No, sir, never did none. None of the rest. Of course, I play piano a little bit, but I never did play enough to do no good.
Harmonica? No, sir, never did none. Pazoo. Okay. Just a pazoo. Just a pazoo. Okay. How come they call you Hog Man?

Well... That was kind of a short name that they gave me. They was, uh... I always believed that I was a hog doctor and I... So I started off doctoring on hogs, and every time Dad would get a bunch of pigs and they'd leave home, I'd give a hog doctor. So I messed around, I think I killed about half of them, and they named me the Hog Man behind. Ha, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha. I always figured that the one needed operating on. I figured that I was to put a good hand to operating, so when they'd leave home, I'd give a hog operating. Every time they'd leave home, I had to operate on two, three of them that had to penny-sided. So I messed around and I operated on two minutes to begin to get skates, and so they'd begin the check on it and they found out I was the doctor, so they just named me the Hog Man behind.
Ha, ha, ha, ha, ha. Ha, ha, ha, ha. That's a, uh, not to get personal or anything, but, uh... Ha, ha, ha, ha, ha. Ha, ha, ha, ha.

So after then, I kind of slacked up on, uh, after they got through talking to me around in the smokehouse, nobody there but me and them, so I kind of lightened up on doctoring on the hogs so much. They doctored on me, but the only thing, they didn't use no knife. They didn't use the wooden knife with the doctor don't be with it, so I quit doctoring on the hogs, so they gave me the name of the Hog Man. So I've been wearing it off and on ever since Hog Man. Yeah. I wanted to ask you,
uh, how long have you been here at Angola?

I've been here, I've gone on four years now. And how much more time do you have? Well, I had to do seven, ten, fifteen. Seven, ten? Seven, ten, fifteen. I had nine years. Uh-huh. And I do seven, ten, fifteen only. What's seven, ten, fifteen? Well, I do seven years, ten months, fifty days. Oh. I see. Without any, you know, unless I get some consideration on some of the pardon rules, and I won't, probably if I get some of it cut, well, I won't have it. If I get any cut, well, the more they cut off, well, the less I have to do in the seven years.
Have you ever been in any other place?
Well, uh, I've never been in no other place,
but just... How many times have you been here? The second time. This is your second time. I broke my parole
and came back here. Uh-huh.
Oh. So it's for one offense, so basically... Oh, it's just
two different offenses.

Two different offenses. Two different offenses. What are you in for? Well, we'll go through that further later. Okay, we'll talk about that later. All right. All right. Yeah, well, we... I just wanted to know the information for the parole boy and stuff, you know? Well, the other one... We've got to have the background. We can get that on the records, but I'd rather have it in your own voice, you know? Yeah, yeah. And did you hear many guitar players here? Well, I haven't had
so many here. We had, I think it was three or four here pretty good, and something went with them. I think they went home someplace. I missed them.
Did you know Lightning when he was here?
Lightning, Lightning left before. I knowed him, but I never did get to hear him play too much.
I heard him play
a while at eight.
What was his name, Lightning?
We just called him Lightning. I didn't know what his name was.

His name is, that's what you say, well, it's Winfield Williams? Winfield Williams. Yeah, everybody called him Lightning because he got lightning struck. Lightning what? Lightning hit it. He did? Yes. And where is he now?
In Baton Rouge, last I heard from him.
And he's still playing guitar in Baton Rouge.
When I was out on parole, I played a couple of night club with him. Uh-huh.
Yes. He and Ball in all night. I was listening last night. He was just on the other band that was having a battle with the blues. He was them BB King, Muddy Waters, and all.
Is that the guy they call Lightning Hopkins?
Oh, Lightning Hopkins was in Houston. Oh, yeah.
Well, I know

he's over there. They don't play nothing like Lightning Hopkins. That's a lot different than the way they're playing Lightning Hopkins. Man, they'll never reach him. Yeah. Yes, they didn't play but they're too like him. That man, it's terrible. He is. He is that. Yeah. You don't find me nothing playing like he do. He swaps sides. He got two guitar. He played left-handed while he didn't play right-handed. I haven't heard of that. He played either side.
Let's get his strength down for the boy. Well, yeah, we'll be true.
Say it up. Yeah. How about the run that Christmas blue? All right. All right. Run it back while I'm talking as well. We'll get over
here in the corner, okay?
Hey, the run. I just want to live in the middle of this through the old

feet. See some more. Where else have you been? You've been in Angola twice, you say? Yes, sir. A year twice. And how many years is the first time? First time I had 15. 15? Yes. Next time I had 20. And now how much do you have left?

Well, I just about started on the 20. I haven't got about four years on the 20 story. See, I left eight years on my road. I came back and finished that and started. I got three years on my on my 20. The 18th of next month, I'll be back four years. I mean, I'll be done and done four years. Otherwise, I've been back here nine years 16, 18th of next month.
And have you been in any place else? Yes, I was in Mississippi. In Mississippi. Where was that? Parchman, Mississippi. Have many good guitar players there? Well,

they had one or two. Otherwise, they wasn't interested. They wasn't interested. At that time, they wasn't interested in the music. The only thing they was interested in those girls to come to see them every Sunday and Saturday would be with them until Monday.
And they let them visit over there? Yes, sir. Well, that's a much better plan, I think. possible. And they would always

be interested in the girls playing baseball. Oh, yeah. You know, there's three or four of them get out there sometimes with estimates and draw the gang and make them drums and water and play the game. Yeah.
I guess if you've got enough women, you don't need to play the blues. You said that right. You know how that is. Yeah, I know. Yeah, yeah, he did. Uh,
how long were you in
Forchman? 21 months and nine days. In other words, it was called two years since.
Uh-huh.
So, you're at least out of that. Yes, sir. Yes, sir.
Wow.
Hope we can do something with the board. Well,

the pardon board called me up this morning, signed some papers. So, I signed and they were going to carry me on the next month's board. And they promised me they was going to help me. So, with y'all helping theirs and other friends y'all on the farm I got, I recommend them, I believe I make sure.
Now, what about in Forchman? Did they sing those work songs over
there, sir? Yes, sir.
That's how I learned it. That's how I learned

those songs that I know here. But, when I came here, they were singing them over here, too. Same songs or different? Same songs, yes, sir. That's practically in every penitentiary you go. That same old song, that's a sturdy lick hit. You get that song and you just work steady all day. One be tired, one be thankful. You just got a sturdy lick. One behind you, you're ball up, raising our shoveling thing at the same time. Just like that. Some singing. In other words, sometimes they have one or two men leading the game. They don't be doing anything, but you singing. You know that's keeping up.
You've been a lead man, huh?
Yes, sir, I've been a lead man, and I've been on the tail end, been in the middle and all.
You know the ropes, huh? Yes, sir. Let's see, he's next. Let me get you a little bit on him, now. We want to know about your sons, here.
How long you got? I'm done live. You're doing live, live. I've been here on this live. I'll be here, I'll be to see the next month. Six, three years. Three years.

Be here three years. Three years, six the next month. And this is your first time in annual? First time, I was in trouble. First time you ever been in trouble and you got lied. Yes, got lied. Oh, yes.

Well, I got this live here. I walked in the store, had a beer garden on the side of the store, you know? And two fellows leaning up on the bar and one of them asked me why that I came from. And I told him I came from Zachary. Well, he cussed me a time or two and told me I didn't come to Zachary. I told him, yes, I did. So he cussed me again. I said, well, I wouldn't call you that. So he said, let me tell you one thing. He said, you better go back to Zachary and pick some more cut, because you want to do slicker. I said, well, I don't have to do that. So I walked on for me by a runner, where I know the fellow was, standing up at the table. I said, say, David, give me a beer. He said, there's a whole quart, help you sell. So David went and got me a paper cup, and I still drank some beer with him. So this fellow, Lee, Jackie, he came over there while we was. And that made three of us at the table. My sister's brother and I the dough. So this fellow said, you see that guy yonder? Fellow leaned up by the bar, said, yeah. He said, doesn't come in with the suit on? He said, no, that's not this guy you're talking with. He said, yeah. He said, watch me mess him up before daylight. Well, he wasn't talking that kind of talk, but he was talking with it. So, you know, some people take a hint, you know. I said to myself, I better get out of here. This guy might when I went to walk out, these fellows started waiting to table with me. He saw that I was going and he made a break over there, one of those hot bill knives that cut that roof and paper with. Well, he grabbed me, but I told him it was funny. People saw that the rookies started, well, they jumped up for a run, but they got the dough blocked. After he hadn't blocked the dough, I mean, I could have got out and I couldn't get out, I was in the jam, so, well, I hit my side, so he said, well, you just got to do it. Well, I see the man to kill me, so I shot him in the stomach, but he never stopped, he was too close on me to even fall. And the next shot I shot him, I didn't know why I hit him, but it hit him up there around chest or heart somewhere, well, that's what killed him. Well, it didn't kill him right then, they take him to the hospital, but he died a few minutes after he got in the hospital. And I left, went to my car, and this fellow, David Thomas, told me, he said, give me your pistol. I said, no, I ain't gonna give you my gun. I turned that to the law. By me, he had never been in trouble. It my family came on to the house. Sitting out on the porch smoking a cigarette. The law came up there. Mr. White, he knows me. He hollered, Pete, and I said, yes, sir. He said, put him up. I put my hand up. They came on up there, and they patty me down, put the handcuffs on me, and actually while with the gun, I told them to send the house and my luggage. So they went on there and got the gun. They brought me in the jig. So the same fellow was standing at that table with me, which made three, and two more of the other wasn't at the table. Well, they used five. And I honored the place Bradley that he paid them to go against me. So that's why I'm here now. ! I had one witness Herman Landry. My boss man, he came down there. But it wasn't nothing that he could say but he wasn't there you know. He could just speak for him because he knew what a good record I had and a good worker. So they didn't want to hear my boss man until he put the sign on them then he heard them then . understand. So this fellow Herman Landry the actual what did he know about he told them that when he came round there with one fellow searching him they had taken his knife out of his hand and his watch off his arm and went out the back with it. So that's why they tried to lexicate me because they didn't get no weapons off him. His friend got that. And they paid them to go canceling. So as I got it this way trusting God that will make it. I'll have a chance someday. Now that fellow was standing up there with him. God fixed so that he came right here to the penitentiary. I worked over the milk dairy two years and that fellow kept watching me. He said why did you came from North? He didn't say that. I asked him a couple times. I said why you watching me so hard? He said it seemed like I seen you somewhere. I said well maybe you here. I said you remember some trouble happening down there at Bradley Stoke? He said yeah. I said did you know that fellow that killed that man? He said no I don't. ! ! I said well do you know the fellow that got killed? He said yeah. I said well the fellow that killed him was he in the wrong? He said no he wasn't in the wrong. I said why did that fellow kill this fellow? He said well he said I tell you if he ! killed him he ! killed him kill me you know? ! I said ! why he said because he took him for the wrong man. I said that the way it was he said yeah I said well I tell you that was me had to do that he said looky here he said I could help you out plenty I said how could you help me and I'm here at penitentiary he said well I tell you Bradley paid five of them to go against you that's what he did I said well I wish he had came down and asked that you didn't go against me because spoke for him I would help him because my life was sweeter to me than his than him that was it

she was a real good singer and then I knew her in personally she was raised up there on the syndicates at Scotts Mississippi and I was working at that sawmill at the time she used to give 4th of day July dances and she would she would stay she was staying there but the band would come from Greenville out there and she sang get on the stage and sang for her

segments.title: Tuning the guitar and the nickname Shakey
segments.summary: Mic placement and guitar choice, tuning talk, and Welch explaining his nickname Shakey.

segments.title: Jelly Roll songs and playing the dozens
segments.summary: Interviewer asks about Jelly Roll songs and the dozens; Welch recalls Jelly Roll Blues.

segments.title: Slide playing, kazoo and recording Jazz Bo Boogie
segments.summary: Setting up to record; talk of bottle slides and steel, then Welch plays a kazoo piece.

segments.title: Welch's name, number, birth in Memphis 1896 and Memphis jug bands
segments.summary: Welch gives name, prisoner number and birth in Memphis in 1896; Gus Cannon, Will Shade, Jim Jackson mentioned.

segments.title: Washboard and percussion, Maxey's band earnings and twin sister
segments.summary: Maxey describes hitting a washboard, cowbell rigs, his own band earning $105 an hour, and his musical family.

segments.title: Maxey's name, birth in 1917 and moving as a child
segments.summary: Matthew Maxey gives his name, Hogman nickname, birth in Louisiana in 1917 and moving away at nine.

segments.title: Maxey's musical family
segments.summary: Parents, brothers and sisters of Maxey played violin, guitar and piano; fifteen children.

segments.title: Maxey learns violin then guitar
segments.summary: Maxey describes his first instrument, learning violin from a visitor, starting his own outfit in 1934 and taking up guitar in 1938.

segments.title: Robert Pete Williams: nickname, Zachary birth 1914 and family
segments.summary: Pete Williams gives his nickname and birth in Zachary, Louisiana, in 1914; a sister and uncle play guitar.

segments.title: Building a cigar-box guitar; Maxey's first guitar
segments.summary: Pete began in 1934 on a homemade copper-wire guitar; Maxey recalls starting on a twelve-string.

segments.title: Playing alone with guitar, kazoo and harmonica
segments.summary: Pete repeats his cigar-box guitar story and says he played by himself with guitar and kazoo.

segments.title: Pete wants to quit music for religion
segments.summary: Pete says he considers putting down the guitar for Jesus, was called to preach, and his son preaches.

segments.title: Learning by ear and making up blues
segments.summary: Pete had no teacher, makes blues from sounds in the air, and can make one on any subject.

segments.title: Zachary and Baton Rouge geography
segments.summary: Pete says he left Zachary for Baton Rouge in 1928 and describes the station stops.

segments.title: Pete's favorite guitarist Lacey Collin and listening to records
segments.summary: Pete names Lacey Collin of Elton as favorite and says records do not stick in his head.

segments.title: Welch learns guitar from country suppers and juke-house pianists
segments.summary: Welch learned guitar at his mother's country suppers and from piano players in juke houses.

segments.title: Ernest 44, carrying instruments and brother Tellis Washington's orchestra
segments.summary: Welch learned 44 from Ernest 44, played country suppers, then joined his trombonist brother Tellis Washington's orchestra.

segments.title: Greenville Pepper Shakers and Welch's own Texas band
segments.summary: Welch played with the Greenville Pepper Shakers and led a seven-piece band, playing Louisiana clubs.

segments.chapter: Prison work songs and Lead Belly
segments.title: Lead Belly at Camp A
segments.summary: Welch served time with Lead Belly at Camp A in 1938 and says he only picked up paper in the yard.

segments.chapter: Prison work songs and Lead Belly
segments.title: Prison work songs, lead singers and the nickname Guitar
segments.summary: Welch explains singing while chopping and raking, who leads the row, and being called Guitar.

segments.title: Grandfather's banjo and learning from Papa Charlie Jackson records
segments.summary: Welch learned on his grandfather's banjo and Papa Charlie Jackson records, teaching himself.

segments.title: Grandfather Bob Welch the preacher and Welch's instruments
segments.summary: Welch's preacher grandfather played banjo and his grandmother violin; Welch plays six-string guitar and a bit of piano.

segments.title: How Maxey got the name Hogman
segments.summary: Maxey tells the story of doctoring hogs as a boy, earning the name Hog Man.

segments.title: Maxey's sentences at Angola and guitar players there
segments.summary: Maxey explains his seven-to-fifteen year term, his parole break and the lack of guitarists at Angola.

segments.title: Lightning Winfield Williams and Lightning Hopkins
segments.summary: Maxey discusses Angola's Lightning (Winfield Williams), playing nightclubs with him, and Lightning Hopkins.

segments.title: Tape adjustments
segments.summary: Recording chatter about running the tape.

segments.title: Welch's terms at Angola and Parchman and the pardon board
segments.summary: Welch gives his Angola terms, a stay at Parchman with visiting women, and the pardon board.

segments.title: Work songs at Parchman and Angola
segments.summary: Welch says the same work songs are sung in every penitentiary and that he has been a lead man.

segments.title: Pete Williams's killing and conviction
segments.summary: Pete tells how a bar fight led to a killing, his conviction and a later witness account.

segments.title: Grandfather's songs and learning bottleneck from Frank Banglin
segments.summary: Welch cannot recall grandfather's songs; Frank Banglin taught him bottleneck guitar.

segments.title: Records Welch heard and Bessie Smith
segments.summary: Welch lists blues records he heard (Papa Charlie Jackson, Blind Lemon, Lonnie Johnson, Ma Rainey) and names Bessie Smith as favorite, claiming to have seen her sing in Mississippi.

segments.title: Bud Scott and Welch's seven-piece band
segments.summary: Welch recalls Bud Scott's large orchestra competing with his band and his singing style.

segments.title: Bessie Smith songs, memory and Shake Him On Down
segments.summary: Welch says he has forgotten many songs; interviewer asks for Shake Him On Down before leaving.
